subject: olive sea snake
title: A Venomous Sea Snake Chases Divers. Scientists Finally Know Why

scenes.text: A deadly sea snake chases divers. It isn't hunting them.
scenes.keywords: olive sea snake swimming coral reef

scenes.text: The olive sea snake, Great Barrier Reef. Its bite can kill, and it swims straight at scuba divers.
One diver logged every meeting in 1994 and 95. In 74 of 158, the snake came to him.
Thirteen were charges, all in breeding season, by males who'd just lost a female they were chasing.
Three males even coiled around the diver's fin, a move snakes use in courtship.
So it isn't hunting. It's hitting on you.

description:
Olive sea snakes on the Great Barrier Reef swim straight at scuba divers, and a 2021 study in Scientific Reports found out why.
A diver recorded every encounter in 1994 and 1995: snakes approached in 74 of 158 meetings, most often from May to August, the breeding season. Thirteen encounters were rapid charges, all in the mating season, and the charging males had just lost an unsuccessful chase of a female or a fight with a rival. Three males coiled around the diver's fin, behaviour normally seen in courtship. The snake is venomous and potentially lethal, but it was not attacking: it had mistaken the diver for a mate.
Would you stay still if a sea snake wrapped around your fin?
first_comment: The researchers' advice: don't flee. A snake that thinks you're a rival or a mate loses interest if you keep still. Would you manage that?
